candidates.title: RESILAGENT: A Three-Pillar Architecture for Cyber-Physical Resilience in Electrical Power and Energy Systems
candidates.abstract: Electrical Power and Energy Systems face hybrid threats that combine cyber intrusions, physical sabotage and climate-driven stress, and routinely outpace today's siloed monitoring stacks. We present RESILAGENT, a concept architecture organised around three operational pillars, Sensing & Data Intelligence, Resilience Analytics & Reporting, and Incident Response & Recovery, mediated by a Cloud-based Orchestrator and exercised through a closed Detect-Simulate-Decide-Sign loop. The framework fuses agentic artificial intelligence and multimodal large language models for cross-modal detection, real-time digital twins for what-if simulation, and a permissioned blockchain anchor for tamper-evident threat intelligence and CER/NIS2-aligned evidence. We instantiate it on two scenarios, a transmission operator under coordinated cyber compromise, sabotage and heatwave, and a distribution operator under a supply-chain compromise during a storm, and report an IEEE-bus micro-benchmark that quantifies each pillar through false-data-injection attack detection, cyber-physical fusion lift, N-1 contingency screening and anchor cost.

candidates.title: A Matter of Stages: Energy-Latency Trade-offs in Multimodal LLM Serving
candidates.abstract: Online serving of multimodal large language models requires deciding whether to separate visual encoding (E), prefill (P), and decode (D) across GPUs and how to configure their frequencies. EPD disaggregation enables independent stage control, but it also changes communication and queueing behavior. Lowering one stage's frequency can increase queueing and prolong execution across the EPD pipeline. Consequently, reducing power at one stage does not necessarily reduce total GPU energy per request. In this paper, we systematically characterize fused and EPD-disaggregated serving across four multimodal models under a fixed three-GPU budget, followed by single-stage and uniform downclocking experiments across 18 workload combinations. We find that disaggregation reduces GPU energy per successful request by 13.3-37.0% at nearly identical output-token throughput, but increases mean TTFT. Downclocking exhibits distinct stage sensitivities, and aggressive frequency reductions can offset power savings through queueing and longer execution. Across the evaluated workloads, uniform downclocking to 80% reduces GPU energy by 11.7-18.6% with modest mean-latency changes. Guided by these findings, we develop a budgeted frequency exploration strategy to select energy-efficient configurations under latency constraints. Evaluation shows that four probes can identify the lowest-energy feasible configuration among 25 measured candidates across all 288 evaluated positive-margin SLO scenarios. These results provide practical guidance for energy-efficient multimodal serving.

candidates.title: A Hybrid Systems Approach to Parameterizing the PERC1 Model for Data Centers Using Synchrophasor Measurements
candidates.abstract: The Power Electronic Reconnecting and Ceasing (PERC1) load model represents the timed ceasing and reconnection of large power-electronic loads, including data centers. Voltage thresholds and timers govern its response, with a ramp on reconnection, making it a hybrid dynamical system. This paper formulates PERC1 as a hybrid automaton and uses that structure to identify its parameters from synchrophasor records of grid disturbances. We propose a four-stage identification procedure: mode-sequence identification, estimation of logic parameters from event-time constraints, and joint Gauss-Newton refinement using hybrid trajectory sensitivities and saltation matrices. The resulting salted Fisher information is then used to analyze parameter identifiability. Two structural results are established. The detection and actuation delays are identifiable only through their sum unless a second dip interrupts the reconnection ramp, and a single disturbance leaves one unidentifiable direction in each threshold-delay pair, which two disturbances with different voltage slopes resolve. A case study using synthetic 60 frames/s synchrophasor records demonstrates recovery of the ceasing and reconnection dynamics and identifies poorly observable parameters.

candidates.title: Investigating the Impact of CI-Source Sensitivity in Carbon-Aware Resource Management Systems
candidates.abstract: The sustainable growth of data centres increasingly depends on Resource-Management Systems (RMSs) that aim to reduce carbon emissions of computing workloads without degrading performance. This need is intensified by the rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI) workloads, which demand exponentially growing amounts of compute and energy across geographically distributed infrastructure. Recent carbon-aware RMSs exploit temporal and spatial variation in grid Carbon Intensity (CI) to shift workloads towards lower-carbon periods or locations. In practice, CI estimates and forecasts can be inaccurate and uncertain, and CI providers' methods differ substantially. Such discrepancies may have a significant impact on RMS placement decision-making, raising concerns about the fragility of existing solutions. Thus, in this work, we ask how discrepancies between plausible CI estimates propagate into resource-management decisions and operational outcomes. To answer this question, we harmonise and characterise CI traces from Wattnet and ElectricityMaps across five Central European zones. We then propose our evaluation framework: External CI Signal Characterisation And Perturbation Evaluation (ESCAPE), which assesses provider switching and controlled CI perturbations in a reproduced placement setting. We implement our framework using CarbonEdge as a use case, and measure changes in placement decisions and operational outcomes, such as carbon proxy, energy use, and latency. Our results show that switching CI-source changes the dominant placement site in 43.50% cases, and alters reported operational outcomes. These changes occur despite high rank correlation and structured disagreement between CI-sources. This observed sensitivity to CI-source choice motivates robustness-aware carbon-aware placement, in which CI uncertainty should be explicitly accounted for in resource-allocation decisions.

candidates.title: NL2RCtrl: Risk-Controlled Controller Synthesis from Natural Language Requirements
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled the translation of natural language (NL) requirements into linear temporal logic (LTL) specifications, facilitating controller synthesis for cyber-physical systems (CPSs). However, the reliability of such translations remains a concern in safety-critical applications, particularly when NL requirements are ambiguous. This paper proposes a framework based on Conformal Risk Control (CRC) to provide a statistical guarantee on the risk of issuing a controller that violates the user's intended requirement. Rather than requiring semantic equivalence between the generated and intended specifications, the proposed approach considers language inclusion, a sufficient condition for ensuring that the traces of a controller synthesized for the generated specification satisfy the intended requirement. To account for ambiguity, the LLM is queried multiple times, and the resulting LTL specifications are grouped into semantic equivalence classes and ranked by their frequency of occurrence. Given a prescribed risk level, CRC selects how many of the top-ranked equivalence classes to combine into a single LTL specification, such that the probability of issuing a controller that violates the intended requirement is bounded by that level. A controller is then synthesized for the resulting specification, or the framework abstains. Experiments on a vehicle navigation case study evaluate the proposed approach.

candidates.title: Benchmarking LLM Inference on Desktop-Scale NVIDIA Grace Blackwell Clusters
candidates.abstract: Two NVIDIA DGX Spark GB10 systems connect directly over 200 GbE to serve larger language models and increase inference capacity, but the benefits depend on how they are deployed. We benchmark 17 open-weight checkpoints spanning dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, 8B to 235B parameters and four weight precisions on one and two RDMA-connected systems. Using vLLM, we compare tensor parallelism (TP=2), pipeline parallelism (PP=2) and a two-replica baseline at concurrency 1 to 64, with three independent launches per configuration. TP=2 delivers a median 1.59x peak-throughput gain over one Spark, versus 1.39x for PP=2 and has higher throughput in 93 of 96 matched comparisons with separated 95% Welch intervals. It reduces unloaded inter-token latency to 0.52x to 0.73x of one Spark, whereas PP=2 provides little reduction. TP=2 also achieves the highest goodput under a strict 100 ms inter-token latency objective wherever both strategies are supported and the objective is met. For models fitting on one Spark, TP=2 generally favors low-concurrency serving, while replication offers higher throughput at high concurrency. One Spark uses less GPU energy per output token at matched concurrency. Across three precision ladders, NVFP4 reduces unloaded latency more than adding a second Spark at BF16. NCCL microbenchmarks and comparisons with an earlier TCP campaign suggest that collective communication overhead contributes to the advantage of TP=2. These results provide deployment guidance for desktop-scale inference.

candidates.title: Locational Marginal Pricing of Compute: Co-optimizing Compute and Energy for Transparent Data Center Flexibility
candidates.abstract: Demand from data centers and AI compute is growing rapidly and is increasing stress on the power grid. This load could be flexible through user adjustments and provide relief during energy scarcity events, yet today its flexibility is provided through utility call-ups or system-operator load shedding, and is invisible to the users whose workloads are being curtailed. In this work, we propose to quantify and couple the prices of compute and energy in a single optimization problem. The resulting compute price reflects the marginal cost of the binding constraints and decomposes into components indicating which grid, power, hardware, or service requirement causes a price surge. The economic interpretation updates the price with real-time conditions and gives users a signal for potential flexibility provision. The co-optimization ultimately connects compute and energy markets while providing a signal for relief of stress on both the grid and the compute resources.

candidates.title: The Grid's Own Language: A Common Information Model Layer for LLM Grid Assistants
candidates.abstract: Assistants built on large language models (LLMs) are entering power system operation. Current designs delegate computations to validated solvers, but the agent still infers the type, role and state of each element from its name and tool-specific formats, and errors propagate to every study. The Common Information Model (CIM), the IEC standard in which operators already exchange network models, defines unambiguously what each element is and how it connects. We propose a CIM layer for LLM grid assistants and implement it in CONDUCTOR, an open-source assistant. Both the agent and its power-system studies read the layer. It labels the provenance of each fact (stated in the data, suggested only by a name, or inferred from topology), loads operators' CGMES models directly, and builds in $\leq$1\,s on the 9,241-bus PEGASE network. Deterministic checks compare every answer with solver results and the layer. On 37 tasks about the CIGRE medium-voltage and IEEE 30-bus networks, the agent gets right 97\,\% of the graded facts with the layer, such as a unit's energy source or a switch's normal state, against 55\,\% without it. We argue that a CIM layer should be a default component of grid assistants.

candidates.title: Large Language Model-based Optimization for Wireless Communication: A Survey
candidates.abstract: The growing complexity and dynamism of modern wireless communication frameworks have made real-time optimization essential for efficient resource allocation. Traditional optimization and machine-learning techniques often struggle with generalization, adaptability, stability, and scalability in heterogeneous, time-varying environments. Large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as powerful tools capable of reasoning over structured prompts and generating context-aware decisions in real time without domain-specific retraining. This survey provides a comprehensive review of LLM-driven optimization techniques applied to wireless communication problems such as power control, bandwidth allocation, task offloading, and intelligent surface configuration. We introduce a functional taxonomy of LLM-enabled wireless resource management strategies and analyze the prompt engineering methodologies employed in recent literature. Furthermore, we develop a generalized analytical framework that categorizes LLM-based optimization architectures, including direct solution generation, closed-loop optimization with external verifiers, and representation encoding within trainable neural pipelines. To demonstrate practical applicability, we present representative case studies on LLM-assisted beam prediction for millimeter-wave systems and adaptive wireless resource allocation. Finally, we discuss emerging hybrid AI approaches for wireless networks.

candidates.title: IA-MoE: An Intensity-Aware Mixture of Experts for DNN Inference
candidates.abstract: With the ever-increasing parameter scale and structural complexity of deep neural network (DNN) models, traditional cloud-based inference encounters bottlenecks in performance, privacy protection, and energy efficiency. While edge computing and edge intelligence facilitate the migration of inference tasks to edge servers closer to the data source, existing end-edge-cloud collaborative inference still encounters critical challenges, such as sensitivity to heterogeneous resources, complexity in multi-objective optimization, and adaptability to dynamic workloads. To achieve the joint optimization of end-to-end latency and energy consumption under dynamic inference requests with multi-resource constraints, we propose IA-MoE, an intensity-aware Mixture of Experts (MoE) framework. By modeling the model partitioning problem as a bilateral matching problem between layer tasks and virtual machine resources for each inference request, IA-MoE dynamically partitions DNN models in an edge-cloud hybrid computing environment. We evaluate IA-MoE using three representative DNNs (i.e., AlexNet, VGG16, ResNet50) on two public inference datasets in an enhanced CloudSimSDN simulation environment. Experimental results demonstrate that IA-MoE outperforms baseline methods regarding weighted normalized metrics for end-to-end latency and energy consumption. To our knowledge, this is the first study to introduce the MoE paradigm for DNN partitioning and collaborative inference in hybrid computing environments, providing a practical solution for efficient inference in artificial intelligence applications.

candidates.title: Low-Voltage Ride-Through in AI Data Centers via Coordinated Battery and Computing Load Control
candidates.abstract: The ability of large AI data centers to ride through grid voltage sags is critical to power system stability and reliability. This paper frames data center low-voltage ride-through (LVRT) as a DC-link power balance problem. Once the rectifier reaches its current limit, the power drawn from the grid decreases in proportion to the grid voltage. The DC-link capacitor can supply the resulting power deficit only briefly before the DC-link voltage falls low enough to trigger undervoltage protection tripping. To address this issue, this paper proposes effective control strategies for coordinating uninterruptible power supply (UPS) battery and computing load curtailment to offset the power deficit and enable LVRT at minimum control cost. Three control scenarios are studied: UPS battery support alone, computing load curtailment alone, and the coordinated use of both resources. Electromagnetic transient (EMT) simulations using the TAMU-ERCOT AI data center model demonstrate that battery support and the coordinated strategy achieve LVRT for all tested sags, including a near-zero-voltage fault, while load curtailment alone rides through moderate voltage sags.

candidates.title: AC Assessment of DC Power Flow Screening for Data Center Hosting Capacity and Siting
candidates.abstract: A screening procedure based on direct current (DC) power flow estimates the data center hosting capacity of a candidate bus, termed the DC-screened capacity, and selects the generator commitment that supports it. This paper assesses that estimate under the alternating current (AC) network model. With the selected commitment fixed, an AC optimal power flow reoptimizes dispatch and voltages to find the largest data center load the bus can carry, termed the AC-assessed capacity. On a synthetic Texas system with 123 buses, the DC-screened capacity exceeds the AC-assessed capacity at 113 buses. Across all 123, the ratio of DC-screened to AC-assessed capacity has a median of 143% (a 43% overestimate) and a maximum of 1,070%. At these 113 buses, the DC-screened capacity violates a branch apparent power limit or a generator reactive power limit in the AC model, two limits the DC model omits. The overestimate changes decisions: a 1-GW project passes DC screening at every bus but exceeds the AC-assessed capacity at 37, and the bus ranked first by DC screening has 205.5 MW less AC-assessed capacity than the bus ranked second. Reporting the AC-assessed capacity beside each DC-screened capacity lets planners reject oversized projects or choose better sites.

candidates.title: From Sensors to Silicon: Causal Cross-Layer Self-Healing Edge AI for Secure and Energy-Adaptive IoT Systems
candidates.abstract: The migration of artificial intelligence from centralized cloud infrastructure to resource-constrained Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices reduces communication latency and improves data locality, but it also tightly couples sensing quality, inference behavior, microarchitectural activity, hardware reliability, security, and energy management within the same physical node. Existing edge-intelligence solutions predominantly address these dimensions in isolation, making it difficult to determine whether an observed degradation originates from sensor malfunction, data-distribution shift, malicious execution, hardware faults, or resource and thermal stress. This paper presents a causal cross-layer self-healing Edge-AI framework that continuously observes synchronized telemetry spanning sensor health, inference uncertainty, processor hardware-performance counters, accelerator and memory activity, power and thermal state, and communication conditions. A temporally informed causal reasoning engine estimates the most probable origin of abnormal behavior and quantifies diagnostic uncertainty, including under concurrent perturbations.

candidates.title: AI Inference-Aware Optimal Power Flow: Converting Token Requirements into Grid Flexibility
candidates.abstract: The rapid growth, temporal variability, and geographic concentration of electricity demand from artificial intelligence (AI) inference can aggravate transmission congestion near data centers (DCs). The spatial and temporal flexibility of inference workloads offers an opportunity to alleviate this congestion: requests can be routed across DCs or deferred within users' quality-of-service (QoS) requirements. However, inference routing primarily considers graphics processing unit (GPU) availability, leaving this flexibility underused in grid operation. Using GPU measurements, this paper models inference latency and DC power consumption to quantify the flexibility available under users' time-to-first-token (TTFT) and inter-token latency (ITL) requirements. These models are then incorporated into an AI inference-aware optimal power flow (OPF) that coordinates inference routing and power system operation among DC operators, the transmission system operator, and inference users. By linking user requests, token generation at DCs, and electricity delivery through the transmission network, the formulation schedules inference workloads subject to both users' QoS requirements and transmission constraints. Simulations on the PJM system show that, compared with computing-based routing and with electricity price-based routing, coordinating inference routing with network operation enables growing DC electricity demand deliverable to be met at lower cost.

candidates.title: Can Agentic LLMs Write Task-Based Parallel Code? A Study of OpenMP Tasking, HPX, StarPU and TTG
candidates.abstract: Task-based programming offers more expressive power than loop-level parallelism, but the runtimes providing it differ widely in API style, maturity, and the amount of public code to learn from. This paper asks how well LLM agents write C++ for four of them: OpenMP Tasking, HPX, StarPU, and TTG. Instead of single one-shot prompts, we use an agentic workflow in which the model edits files, compiles, and runs its kernels until it reproduces a reference output. Five locally hosted open-weight LLM implement seven HPC kernels, including matrix multiplication, Cholesky and LU factorization, in all four frameworks and a serial baseline to verify their understanding of the problem in general. Every kernel is evaluated independently for correctness at each concurrency level, strong scaling, and peak memory. Model capability dominates the outcome: three models produce correct, genuinely task-parallel kernels in 57-82% of the cases, while two models rarely compile their own code and almost never succeed. For the capable models, OpenMP Tasking and HPX are handled most reliably, StarPU is close behind, and TTG trails. The best generated GEMM and factorization kernels match or exceed the multithreaded OpenBLAS/LAPACK reference. However, correctness overstates parallel quality: several "parallel" kernels contain no parallelism at all; and serialized task graphs and unsuitable task granularity remain common.

candidates.title: Job-Level Workload Allocation for Data Centers Under Flexible Interconnections
candidates.abstract: Flexible interconnections allow data centers to connect to the grid sooner without upgrading the grid infrastructure, if they accept limits on their grid power during periods of grid stress. When a limit is reached, the data center must slow some of its computing jobs. This choice sets the cost of flexibility, because the work done by a job is worth far more than the energy it uses. This paper models how jobs respond when their power is reduced, and proposes a real-time method that shares the available power among jobs according to their value. It also gives grid planners a simple measure of how much power a data center can reduce, and for how long. A one-year case study of a 100-MW data center shows that the proposed method lowers the cost of meeting grid limits, and that on-site generation and storage lower it further.

candidates.title: Model-Free UPS Control Tuning for Improved Low-Voltage Ride-Through in AI Data Centers
candidates.abstract: Voltage sags can trigger protection trips in uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems, abruptly reducing the power that AI data centers draw from the grid. This paper improves the low-voltage ride-through (LVRT) capability of AI data centers equipped with double-conversion UPS systems by tuning their existing converter controls. We formulate a bound-constrained optimization problem to maximize the ride-through area, defined as the integral of ride-through time over a range of retained grid voltages. To solve this problem, we develop a batched projected zeroth-order optimization algorithm with adaptive moment estimation (BPZO-Adam). The algorithm evaluates candidate control settings using only simulated ride-through times, making it suitable for vendor-supplied black-box models. Simulations using the TAMU-ERCOT electromagnetic transient (EMT) AI data center model show that tuning converter control parameters increases the ride-through area by 10.6\%. In a separate study, tuning the controls yields a larger ride-through area than increasing the DC-link capacitance tenfold.

candidates.title: Coordinating Distributed AI Servers with Industrial Loads to Reduce Grid-Interconnection Needs
candidates.abstract: We show that co-locating distributed AI servers with industrial demand and coordinating AI workloads with production loads can substantially reduce the additional grid interconnection that AI computing requires. Grid interconnection is increasingly constraining the expansion of large AI data centers. Factories already have grid connections sized for their peak production loads, and we propose hosting AI servers during production valleys. We formulate a joint optimization that sizes CPU and GPU servers, schedules deadline-constrained tasks, and routes tasks among factories, and use it to compare three factory-site architectures with new large data centers serving the same demand. Applying this framework to 31 Chinese manufacturing industries, we find that AI demand and production loads often do not peak together. As a result, AI servers placed at factories and scheduled according to production peaks need about 60% less additional interconnection capacity than new large data centers, and 98% less when tasks are routed among a group's factories.
